n=61: "Main is who the Intro meeting should carry as participants"
c1 declarative is subject n1 (Main); n2 "who"; n3 the Intro meeting; c2 declarative auxiliary should verb carry subject n3 complement n2 (who); r1 "as" c2→n4 (participants); r2 c1→c2.

Hmm, "who the Intro meeting should carry as participants" — the clause c2 opens with "who" held as complement n2. Per settled case: a clause opening with a question word inside another clause states: declarative and tied. Good.

Is "who" as complement fine? "The Intro meeting should carry who as participants" — "who" as complement. Plausible.

L8.

n=62: "turn bold on for characters 10 to 15 of Body"
c1 imperative turn modifier bold modifier on; r1 "for" c1→n1 (characters); n2 "10"; n3 "to 15" (dep "to", head "15")!; r2 "of" n1→n4 (Body); r3 n1→n2; r4 n2→n3.

Hmm: n3 = "to 15" with "to" as a DEPENDENT of "15". "to" is a linking word held as a dependent → L3 ("A linking word is held as a modifier or a dependent").

Hmm, or is "10 to 15" handled as a range nominal? The case "Two bare nouns side by side after a marker: either may be head" — not. Here "to" is a preposition/linking word joining two numbers. Held as a dependent of "15" → it's a linking word held as a dependent. Per L3 that fails.

Hmm, but "to" in "10 to 15" — is it a linking word or part of a range phrase? It is a preposition-like word. The rule: "A linking word is held as a modifier or a dependent" = L3. So reject n=62, quote 'to 15'? Note: "'to' is a linking word held as a dependent of '15', so the range is not tied".

Hmm, but could "to" be a fixed-phrase part? "10 to 15" is a range; the schema has no range wire. Hmm, similar to "and" between modifiers case ("the schema has no wire for that pair") which allows discourse. But the rules' settled case only allows discourse for conjunctions. For "to"...

Hmm, the case list says "So is a conjunction between two modifier words of one clause ('flat and dry'): the schema has no wire for that pair." — "so is a conjunction ... discourse". A relation with marker "to" from n2 (10) to n3 (15) would be the natural handling. Holding "to" as a dependent of "15" — per L3 fails.

Alternatively accept as a number-pair phrase? Hmm.

Let me consider fairness: is this "a wrong statement or lost explicit information"? The range 10 to 15 remains readable ("10" and "to 15"). Hmm. The rule about linking words held as dependents is explicit in L3, and "to" is definitely a linking word. I'll reject L3.

Hmm, but I want to be careful not to over-reject. Let me tally how many rejections I have so far: n=7, 10, 12, 13, 16, 18, 19, 22, 23, 27, 29, 35, 37, 41, 43, 44, 45, 47, 48, 54, 57, 62... That's a lot (22 of 150 by line 72). Rejection rate ~30% by mid-packet. Hmm, that's plausible for formalizer output? Unknown. The instructions warn to judge fairly and accept plausible readings. Let me be careful with borderline ones. I'll revisit the borderline list at the end.

n=63: "a pointed for me, ear olive"
n1 head "a"; c1 fragment modifier pointed complement n1; r1 "for" c1→n2 (me); n3 "ear olive" (dep ear, head olive); r2 n1→n3.

Garbled (like n=4, n=38). "a" as a nominal head — hmm, in n=38 "a" was a modifier. Here n1 head "a" with "pointed" as modifier of the clause and a relation "for" to "me". Then "ear olive" nominal tied to n1.

Is "a" as nominal head acceptable? "a" is an article — a word with no content alone. Garbled message. Hmm, "a pointed for me, ear olive" — same family as n=4 "a sad for me, eyebrow yellow default" and n=38 "a looking out for me, eye auburn big". In n=4, "a" was discourse (L2 risk); n=38 "a" was a modifier; n=63 "a" is a nominal head.

For n=63: "a" as a head nominal — nothing says "a" is a thing. Hmm, but garbled. The head being a function word: "The `head` is wrong" (L3)? Ehh. For a garbled message, holding "a" where it stands... Hmm, "a" is not misspelt or unknown; it's an article. An article as a nominal head is a wrong statement (the article belongs with "pointed"/"ear"). Hmm, but which? "a pointed ear, olive"? These garbled messages come from a template like "a pointed ear for me, ... olive".

I'd accept these garbled ones as plausible: no clear wrong statement to quote... Actually for n=63, one could quote 'a pointed' and say the article is held as a head nominal, losing that it belongs with the next word. Hmm.

Given "if you cannot quote the words, the circuit is acceptable" and the fairness instruction, garbled messages with all words placed should mostly pass. I'll accept n=63 as L8. But then consistency: n=4, n=38 also L8. OK.

n=64: "and Claims by month on the revenue trend needs the same yellow fading to red, please"
c1 declarative discourse and, verb needs, discourse please, subject n1 (Claims); r1 "by" n1→n2 (month); r2 "on" ambiguous c1→n3 (the revenue trend); n4 "the same yellow" (deps the, same, head yellow); c2 nonfinite fading subject n4; r3 "to" c2→n5 (red); r4 c1→c2.

"needs the same yellow fading to red" — c1 has no complements! n4 "the same yellow" is only tied to c2 (as its subject), and c2 tied to c1 via r4. So "needs" has no complement written; the thing needed is inside the nonfinite clause. Hmm: "and Claims by month on the revenue trend needs the same yellow fading to red" — the object of "needs" is "the same yellow fading to red". The circuit makes "the same yellow" the subject of "fading" and ties c2 to c1 — that's the same structure as "a participle describing/naming"... The relation r4 c1→c2 with no marker represents the object. Acceptable? It's like "the dog a size bigger"? Hmm.

The reading: "needs [the same yellow [fading to red]]" — the circuit has n4 as subject of nonfinite "fading". The next layer reads "Claims ... needs the same yellow which fades to red". Reasonable. Accept L8.

Hmm, "discourse and" at start — allowed by the case. "please" in discourse — fine.

L8.

n=65: "reschedule Review, 2026-11-18 at 10:00 UTC"
c1 imperative reschedule complement n1 (Review); n2 "2026-11-18"; r1 "at" ambiguous c1→n3 ("10:00 UTC" — dep 10:00, head UTC); r2 n1→n2.

Hmm: "at 10:00 UTC" — n3 with head "UTC" and "10:00" dependent. Hmm, "10:00" is the time and "UTC" the zone: head should be "10:00"? Per "two bare nouns side by side after a marker: either may be the head" — "at 10:00 UTC": the two bare "nouns" are "10:00" and "UTC". So either may be head. Passes.

"2026-11-18" as a nominal tied to Review via r2 — the date tied to the thing. Fine. L8.

n=66: "get the dog on the lawn to chase the cat, and leave everything else in the picture untouched — the way the drawing looks so far"
c1 imperative get complement n1 (the dog); r1 "on" ambiguous c1→n2; r2 "to" c1→c2 (nonfinite chase) complement n3 (the cat); k1 coordination and: c1, c3; c3 imperative leave modifier untouched complement n4 (everything else), complement n6 (the way); r3 "in" n4→n5 (the picture); n7 the drawing; c4 declarative looks modifier so, modifier far, subject n7; r4 n6→c4.

Hmm: "leave everything else in the picture untouched — the way the drawing looks so far": "the way the drawing looks so far" — n6 "the way" as complement of c3 with r4 to c4. Hmm, per n=20 pattern, accepted. "so far" as modifiers of c4 — fine (fixed phrase).

L8.

n=67: long. "for the monthly ops review on Friday I need the revenue trend legible from the back of the conference room, so how about line thinner?; also let's have the marker borders thicker on the revenue trend before we circulate it wider; plus show both grid lines"
c1 interrogative verb "need" modifier legible subject I complement n4 (the revenue trend)!! 

"for the monthly ops review on Friday I need the revenue trend legible..." — "I need the revenue trend legible from the back" — a declarative statement (not a question). c1 form=interrogative → L1 (a clause with a clear declarative form written as interrogative? L1 says "a clear question written as imperative or declarative, or the reverse"). "or the reverse" = a declarative written as interrogative. So L1. Quote: 'I need the revenue trend legible'.

Yes I think that's a clear rejection: c1 is written interrogative but the message's clause is declarative ("I need ...").

Also k1: coordination with "so" and "plus" joining c1, c2, c3, c6 — the "so" joins c1 with c2 ("so how about line thinner?") and "plus" joins c6. Hmm, c2 is a fragment with ellipsis=$c1 — "how about line thinner?" with ellipsis of "need"?? That's odd: "how about line thinner?" doesn't share "need". Hmm, L4? ellipsis on a fragment that shares no verb. Hmm, "how about line thinner" — hmm, per n=47 pattern "how about thinner grid lines" was a fragment; here the formalizer added ellipsis=$c1. Does "how about line thinner" share the verb "need"? "so how about line thinner?" = "so how about [having] line thinner?" — no shared verb with "need". Hmm, but per settled case (n=47 style), ellipsis is optional. Adding a wrong ellipsis → L4? Hmm, L4: "ellipsis on a fragment that shares no verb".

But L1 first. I'll reject L1 for the form.

n=68: "same as last step exept with objects 3 and 4"
c1 fragment modifier same; r1 "as" c1→n1 (last step); n2 "exept"; r2 "with" n2→k1 (objects 3 and 4); n3 objects; n4 3; n5 4; r3 n1→n2; r4 n3→n4.

"exept" is a misspelt "except", held as a nominal head "exept" — hmm, "exept" is a preposition/linking word (except). Held as a nominal → is it "A linking word is held as ... a dependent"? It's a head, not a dependent. Held as a nominal head — "exept" as head of a nominal tied from n1 and to k1 via "with". Hmm.

Options: it's a misspelt word (except) — held where it stands, when words don't settle. Hmm, the words do settle it's "except"? "except with objects 3 and 4" — the segment "exept with objects 3 and 4" — has the "with" as marker. Hmm.

Is holding "exept" as a nominal head a wrong statement? It makes "exept" a thing ("same as last step [exept] with objects 3 and 4"). Hmm. The information "except" (exclusion) is arguably preserved by the word itself standing there. A next layer sees "exept" and can interpret.

But the rule "A misspelt or unknown word, held where it stands, when the words do not settle what it is" — "exept" is misspelt and it stands where it stands. Passes. L8? Hmm, holding it as a nominal head — "held where it stands" — it stands between "last step" and "with objects 3 and 4", and being a nominal tied there is roughly "where it stands". I'd accept L8.

n=69: "perhaps you could seat a green block in the middle of the top row and in the second column of red blocks"
c1 declarative modifier perhaps, auxiliary could, verb seat, subject you, complement n2; r1 "in" c1→n3 (the middle); r2 "of" n3→n4 (top row); k1 coordination "and" conjunct r1, r3 (relations!); r3 "in" c1→n5 (the second column); r4 "of" n5→n6 (red blocks).

Hmm — k1 coordinates relations r1 and r3. Is coordination of relations allowed? "syntax.coordination: wires put side by side, conjunct`. Rule: "Which earlier wire a coordination joins, when grammar allows several" — the conjuncts are relations; that's allowed? Hmm, "A coordination has a wrong conjunct" (L3). Coordinating the two "in" relations — hmm, the message "a green block in the middle of the top row and in the second column of red blocks" coordinates the two place phrases. Representing each place as a relation and coordinating them: plausible. Hmm, but the second relation r3's "of red blocks"... "of red blocks" – hmm.

Hmm, is "form=declarative" right for "perhaps you could seat a green block..."? It's a request phrased as a statement — declarative form is correct (not interrogative). Good.

Accept L8? The coordination of two relations is unusual but grammar-wise the message coordinates the two prepositional phrases. Accept.

n=70: "draw a small sun partly hidden behind the tree, not in front of it."
c1 imperative draw complement n1 (a small sun); c2 nonfinite modifier partly verb hidden; r1 "behind" c2→n2 (the tree); r2 negation=not marker "in" c2→n3 (front); r3 "of" n3→n4 (it); r4 n1→c2.

"not in front of it" — negation held on the relation r2 — good, negation attribute of a relation exists in the schema. Good. Accept L8.

Hmm, "partly" as modifier of c2, "hidden" verb nonfinite tied to n1 via r4. Good.

L8.

n=71: "put a box between Draft ant Review"
c1 imperative put complement n1 (a box); r1 "between" ambiguous c1→n2 ("Draft ant Review": deps Draft, ant, head Review).

"ant" is a typo for "and" — "Draft and Review" are two things. The circuit holds "Draft", "ant", "Review" as one nominal with head Review. Hmm, that merges two names into one nominal. "between Draft and Review" — two objects. Merged into one nominal → L3 (two nominals merged)? Or is "ant" a misspelt word held where it stands?

Hmm. "between Draft ant Review" — the two ends of "between" should be "Draft" and "Review". Merging them into a single nominal "Draft ant Review" with head "Review" — the "between" relation then has only one end. The information that there are two distinct boxes is lost → L3.

Hmm, but is "ant" an unknown word (misspelt "and")? If the formalizer treats "ant" as an unknown word, it holds it inside the nominal — the case allows misspelt words held where they stand when the words don't settle what it is. But "Draft" and "Review" are two clearly separate names, and merging them into one nominal (head Review, with Draft as dependent) makes "Draft" a description of "Review" — "the Draft Review" — hmm, that's like a two-word name ("Sales 3"), which is allowed! "A name of several words may stand whole in head, or with its last word as head and the others as dependent."

So "Draft ant Review" as a nominal with head "Review" and deps "Draft","ant" is a name-with-typo reading. Hmm. Both "Draft" and "Review" are known names of boxes though. In this dataset (mind maps), "Draft" and "Review" are separate nodes.

Judging: merging two nominals into one is L3. But the words don't settle ("ant" garbles the conjunction) so the name reading is plausible...? Hmm. I think a fair judge would accept this one, since "ant" is unknown and the words are held where they stand — the next layer can read "Draft ant Review" and recover.

Hmm. Ehh. But there's a real loss: "between X and Y" — the two ends. With one nominal, the relation "between" ends at one nominal. Then the next layer gets "between Draft ant Review" as a whole, and can interpret. I'd accept L8 (misspelt word rule).

n=72: "let's have the font smaler on the profit chart and then set the error bar cap size smaller, that's the tweak"
c1 imperative verb let complement n1 ("'s"); c2 nonfinite verb have; c3 nonfinite modifier "the" verb "smaler" complement n2 (font); r1 "on" c3→n3 (profit chart); k1 coordination "and" c2, c4; c4 nonfinite modifier then, verb set, modifier smaller, complement n4 (error bar cap size); n5 that; c5 declarative "'s" subject that complement n6 (the tweak); k2 coordination c1, c5; r2 c1→k1; r3 c2→c3.

Problems: c3 "smaler" — the word "the" held as a modifier of c3, and "smaler" as verb. Hmm: "have the font smaler" — the font is a nominal, "smaler" a modifier. The circuit: c3 nonfinite verb "smaler" with complement n2 "font", modifier "the". That's wrong: "the" is the article of "font"; holding it as a clause modifier splits the nominal (L3: "The words of one nominal are split between wires"). And "smaler" as a verb — a misspelt adjective ("smaller") held as verb → hmm, "A word that grammar allows as a noun or as a verb" doesn't apply. Holding an adjective as the verb — is that L1 ("Its `verb` is a word that is no verb here")? Or L3 (head/modifier wrong).

The cleaner statement: "the" is a modifier of the clause while "font" is a nominal → the nominal "the font" is split → L3. Also "smaler" as verb.

Hmm, which grade? L1: "Its `verb` is a word that is no verb here". "smaler" — misspelt "smaller", an adjective. Could "smaler" be a verb? No. Hmm, but the misspelt-word rule: unknown word held where it stands... held as a verb though; the rule says held where it stands, not necessarily as a verb.

Hmm. L3 for splitting "the font": the rule "The words of one nominal are split between wires" is explicit. Since L1 comes first and might apply ("verb is a word that is no verb"), hmm.

Let me think: c3's verb "smaler" — is "smaler" a word that is no verb here? An adjective in "have the font smaller". So yes, L1 candidate. And the article "the" held as a clause modifier is L3.

I'll go L3 quoting 'the font smaler' and note the nominal "the font" is split ('the' as a clause modifier) and 'smaler' is not a verb... Hmm, but naming the wrong statement matters more than the grade maybe. I'll pick L3 with a note about the split nominal. Hmm.

Hmm, actually — wait. Is c3's structure "have [the font smaler]" where c3 is a nonfinite clause whose verb is "smaler"? Grammatically reading "smaler" as a verb with "font" as object and "the" as modifier — that's a wrong statement about the words: "the" belongs to "font" (article can't be separated from its noun). That's a clear L3 split. Good: L3.

Let me be careful about L1 vs L3 ordering. The instruction: give L8 or "the first of L1 to L6 that applies". If L1 applies, give L1. Does L1 apply? "Its `verb` is a word that is no verb here" — is "smaler" a word that is no verb here? Yes, "smaler" is an adjective (misspelt "smaller"). But the misspelt rule ("an unknown word held where it stands when the words do not settle what it is") could excuse it... "smaler" next to "font" with "the"... the words settle it's the adjective "smaller". Hmm.

I'll go with L1 then? Hmm. Let me weigh which reads as a fairer note. The note can mention both: "'the font smaler' holds 'the' as a clause modifier and 'smaler' as the `verb`, so the nominal 'the font' is split" — with grade L3. That's clear and defensible. But if the reference grade is L1, my grade mismatches.

Given ambiguity and the explicit L3 rule about splitting a nominal, I'll take L3.

Continue reading.

n=73: "instead, a small dog down at the bottom, next clear the top two of the five green blocks, leaving the bottom three exactly as they are — keep the rest as it is"
c1 fragment modifier instead, down, next, **clear**, complement n1 (a small dog), n3 (the top two); r1 "at" c1→n2 (the bottom); r2 "of" n3→n4 (the five green blocks); c2 nonfinite leaving modifier exactly complement n5 (the bottom three); r3 "as" c2→c3 (they are); c4 imperative keep complement n7; r4 "as" c4→c5; k1 coordination c1, c4; r5 n1→c2.

Problem: "next clear the top two ..." — "clear" is the VERB of a command ("clear the top two of the five green blocks"), but it's held as a modifier of the fragment c1. So the command "clear the top two..." has no clause → L5 ("A clause of the message is not written: its verb is held as a modifier ... and no clause has it as verb"). Yes! Clear L5.

Quote: 'next clear the top two' — note: "'clear' is held as a modifier of the fragment, so the command 'clear the top two of the five green blocks' has no clause" → L5.

n=74: "add the Cool, Grind, Sort chain after Sift, arrows and all"
c1 imperative add complement n1 (the Cool Grind Sort chain); r1 "after" ambiguous c1→n2 (Sift); n3 arrows; k1 coordination "and" c1, c2; n4 all; c2 fragment complement k2 ellipsis=c1; k2 coordination n3, n4.

"arrows and all" — c2 fragment with ellipsis=c1 ("add") and complement = coordination of "arrows" and "all". Hmm, "arrows and all" is an idiom meaning "including the arrows". Fine-ish; ellipsis on the fragment saying it shares "add". Acceptable? The fragment "arrows and all" shares "add"? Ambiguous idiom. Hmm, the ellipsis claims it shares the verb "add" — plausible ("add ... arrows and all"). Accept L8.

n=75: "mid-move: object Intro relocates to 260, 240"
c1 declarative modifier mid, modifier move, verb relocates, subject n1 (object Intro); r1 "to" c1→n2 ("260 240": dep 260, head 240).

Acceptable? "mid-move" as two modifiers of the clause — "mid" and "move" as modifiers. Hmm, "mid-move:" is a label ("mid-move"). Held as modifiers of the clause; plausible.

"260, 240" — a coordinate pair. n2 head "240" with dep "260" — hmm, two numbers merged into one nominal. Per the case: "a number or a name right after a noun ('block 2', 'x 120', ...) may be a dependent in that noun's nominal, or a nominal of its own tied to the noun by a relation without a marker." Here 260 and 240 both follow nothing (they're the target). Merging into one nominal with head 240: reads "240 with 260"? The next layer gets both numbers in order. Acceptable-ish → L8.

Hmm, a coordinate pair as one nominal — the rules' examples of number pairs are "x 120". Accept.

n=76: "instead, a small dog down at the bottom, next shift the BMW block down and a little left past the Esso block, lining it up above the Shell block, then shift the BMW block left until it is in line with the Target block below — keep the rest as it is"
c1 imperative modifier instead verb keep complement n11 (the rest)!! That's wrong: "keep the rest as it is" is the last part, but c1 has verb "keep" and modifier "instead" — c1 begins the message? c1 is coordinated via k1 with "then" as conjunction joining c1, c2, c3, c5. So c1 = "instead keep the rest as it is" — the "instead" from the start, "keep" from the end. Hmm, that merges the first word with the last clause. Hmm.

c2 fragment "down" complement n1 (a small dog) with r1 "at" → the bottom. OK.
c3 imperative "next" verb shift modifier down, discourse "and", modifier "a", modifier "little", modifier "left", complement n3 (the BMW block); r2 "past" c3→n4 (the Esso block).
c4 nonfinite lining up complement n5 (it); r3 "above" c4→n6 (Shell block); r8 c3→c4.
c5 imperative shift modifier left complement n7; r4 "until" c5→c6; c6 declarative is subject it; r5 "in" c6→n9 (line); r6 "with" n9→n10 (the Target block below); r7 "as" c1→c7; c7 declarative is subject it (n12).

Words: instead(c1), a small dog n1, down c2, at r1, the bottom n2, next c3, shift, the BMW block n3, down mod, and discourse c3, a little left mods, past r2, the Esso block n4, lining c4, it n5, up mod, above r3, the Shell block n6, then (k1 conjunction), shift c5, the BMW block n7, left mod, until r4, it n8, is c6, in r5, line n9, with r6, the Target block below n10, keep c1 verb, the rest n11, as r7, it n12, is c7.

Big issue: "and a little left" — "and" held as discourse of c3 while it joins "down" and "a little left" (two modifiers). Per the settled case, a conjunction between two modifier words of one clause may be discourse (schema has no wire). OK.

"a" and "little" as modifiers of c3 — "a little left" like "a bit left" — per the case, grading words as modifiers; "a little" may also be a nominal of its own. Fine.

Then "keep the rest as it is": c1 = instead keep the rest as it is, coordinated at the START of the list k1 (c1 first conjunct), where "instead" is the first word. Hmm, that means the "instead" (first word) is in the same clause as "keep the rest" (last part). And "instead" logically belongs to the whole instruction. Is that a wrong statement? Hmm, "Words of one written clause are held in another" — the first part "instead, a small dog down at the bottom" — hmm.

Also, c1 (keep) is placed as the FIRST conjunct of k1 with the conjunction "then" joining c1, c2, c3, c5 — the coordination's conjunctions: "then" appears twice in the message ("then shift the BMW block left") and... "next" is in c3's modifier. k1 has conjunction="then" only once for 4 conjuncts. Hmm, "instead" as modifier of c1, and c1 comes first. The next layer reading the coordination: [keep the rest as it is], [a small dog down at the bottom], [shift the BMW block ...], [shift the BMW block left ...]. Order changed (keep moved to front) — "The order and the names of the wires" are not judged. Hmm, the coordination order isn't judged?

But: "instead" (the first word of the message) is held in the clause of "keep" (the last part) — is that "Words of one written clause are held in another"? The first part "instead, a small dog down at the bottom" has c2 = fragment "down" complement "a small dog". So "instead" belongs to the first part but is in c1. Hmm.

That's a real problem: "instead" (word 1) placed in a clause made of words from the end ("keep the rest as it is"). The clause c1 doesn't exist in the message — "instead ... keep the rest" merges two separated parts. This is a wrong statement: the words of the first part are held in the clause of the last part.

Actually, is it? c1 holds "instead" + "keep the rest as it is". The message: "instead, a small dog down at the bottom, next shift ... — keep the rest as it is". The "instead" is separated by the whole message from "keep". So c1's clause conflates them. L1: "Words of one written clause are held in another." Hmm, c1 isn't a written clause; it's assembled.

Grade? Hmm, maybe L3 ("Words stand in the wrong wire") for "instead". Hmm.

Alternatively focus on a clearer flaw: "then shift the BMW block left until it is in line with the Target block below" — c5 shift modifier left; r4 "until" c5→c6; c6 "it is" ... "in line" — n9 head "line" with r5 "in" from c6. Fine.

"the Target block below" — "below" as dependent of "block": "A word of place after a nominal ('near the lake there', 'the one above') may be a dependent of that nominal or a modifier of the clause" — passes.

Hmm, what about "next shift the BMW block down and a little left past the Esso block" — "next" is held as a modifier of c3 (a word of order as a modifier — allowed: "Now at the start ... may be discourse or a modifier"). "next" as modifier — fine.

So the flaw is the "instead"+"keep" clause. How clear is it? c1 = "instead keep the rest as it is" — the message's last part is "keep the rest as it is" which is a clause of its own; adding "instead" to it (a word from the message's first part) is holding a word of one written clause in another → L1.

Hmm, but "instead" is a discourse-ish word; "which clause holds a discourse word" is NOT judged. If "instead" were a discourse word, its clause wouldn't matter. Here it's a modifier of c1. Hmm, but the rule "Which clause holds a `discourse` word" is not judged — that's for discourse words. "instead" as a modifier of the clause — the rule "A word that grades..." no.

Hmm. Risky. Let me look for other flaws in n=76.

c3's modifiers: down, a, little, left — "shift the BMW block down and a little left" — "down" and "left"; fine.

k1 coordination: conjuncts c1, c2, c3, c5 with "then". Message order: [instead, a small dog down at the bottom], [next shift ...], [then shift ... left ...], [keep the rest as it is]. The coordination joins them; order not judged.

But wait — is c1 an imperative "keep"? yes. So k1 joins imperative clauses; fine.

Hmm. So the "instead" placement is the only flaw. Given "Which clause holds a discourse word" is not judged, and "instead" as a modifier... hmm, but the substantive issue is that c1's clause = "instead keep the rest as it is" is a clause the message doesn't contain — because "instead" belongs to the beginning.

I think a fair judge might accept this: all words placed, structure plausible, next layer can follow. Actually no — the next layer would read "instead keep the rest as it is" as an instruction "instead, keep the rest as it is", and separately "a small dog down at the bottom". The meaning is essentially preserved! "instead" placement doesn't change much. Hmm.
